lines: A reading drifts far from its baseline, the detector fires, and a supervisor stops the line over what was genuinely just the normal ramp after a changeover.
That same false alarm keeps firing all week, until the supervisors stop acting on it entirely, the way anyone eventually tunes out a noise that never means anything.
Then a slow drift arrives, genuinely the one fault that mattered, and it quietly folds right into the baseline without ever once triggering an alarm.
Notice that one failure was firing on something harmless, and the other was staying silent on something that actually mattered; those aren't the same mistake.
What did the design actually get wrong in both directions, and what would a backtest genuinely have shown before any of this ever went live?
answer: A looser threshold on the exact same rule still fires on the ramp, or still misses the drift; the number alone was never the real problem.
The baseline adapted into a fault it should have flagged, and the ramp genuinely needed suppression, not a detector tuned to ignore it a little less.

lines: A line-quality dashboard tolerates seconds of delay, since it's only ever aggregating over a window anyway.
A detector flagging a live measurement has no such patience; what matters there is catching the flag itself, not the exact number attached to it.
What an operator actually does once a flag fires is what sets the real cost of a false alarm against a missed one.
An exponentially weighted average discounts older data as it goes, which is exactly why it adapts smoothly into whatever the series does next.
A seasonal baseline learns the shift, day, and week pattern a line normally follows, so a routine ramp never looks unusual to it at all.
A fixed control-chart limit catches a sudden jump reliably, precisely because it never moves, which is also exactly why it assumes nothing else ever will either.
Every single series out there needs its own baseline state, kept independently in the stream engine's own memory.
A series that just appeared, with barely any history behind it yet, genuinely can't be trusted to alarm on anything at all.
So it stays quiet under a cold-start policy until it actually earns a baseline, or it briefly borrows one from a similar machine nearby.
The same condition firing over and over gets folded into one single alert with its own duration, rather than repeating endlessly.
Alerts that genuinely share one root cause get grouped together under the asset hierarchy, the same grouping idea a data-quality platform already uses for lineage.
A changeover window gets suppressed on purpose, because that ramp was never the anomaly anyone actually needed to hear about.
A detector earns trust by its own precision, and by how much of what it actually flags an operator bothers to act on.
A detector nobody trusts anymore is genuinely worse than having no detector at all, since it still costs attention while returning nothing useful.
Before any detector goes live, it gets replayed straight through history and scored against incidents someone already labelled by hand.
Thresholds get tuned against one period and then genuinely tested against a later one the tuning never touched at all.
That's what would have caught both of this topic's own failures before a single supervisor ever had to live through either one.

Notice what actually closed the gap between a false alarm nobody trusted and a real fault nobody heard: three baselines, each matched to the failure shape it actually suits, and grouping and suppression that keep an alert worth acting on.
And a backtest that proves all of it before anything ever goes live.
The series count here grows by a full order of magnitude.
Each baseline stays exactly as accurate as before, since every series genuinely keeps its own independent state built from nothing but its own history.
So what's actually the next bottleneck?
answer: More series doesn't thin out any single series's own history, so accuracy itself was never actually at risk here.
What genuinely grows right along with the series count is the per-series state's own memory footprint and how fast new series churn through a cold start.
